common_name: Rozannie Aucuba (Compact Self-Fruiting Female Japanese Aucuba)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; unlike most Aucuba japonica cultivars, Rozannie is self-fertile and sets its bright red winter berries without needing a separate male pollinator nearby.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where its solid deep-green, glossy leaves brighten deep-shade spots that stump most flowering shrubs. Rozannie is a compact, dense, rounded female Aucuba japonica selection prized for being reliably self-fertile, so it produces its clusters of glossy scarlet berries through fall and winter on its own, without needing a male plant growing nearby the way most Aucuba cultivars do. Its naturally tidy, mounding habit needs little pruning to stay in bounds, making it a low-maintenance choice for foundation plantings, woodland gardens, and shaded courtyards where year-round structure and winter berry color are wanted. It tolerates deep shade, dry shade once established, and heavy clay better than most broadleaf evergreens, and it is notably resistant to deer browsing.

common_name: Cerise Queen Yarrow (Cherry-Pink Cottage Garden Yarrow)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, surface-sowing since yarrow seed needs light to germinate, or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Cerise Queen tolerates poor, dry soil and needs no fertilizer to thrive.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; rich soil or too much water leads to floppy, weak-stemmed growth in this drought-tough native selection. Cerise Queen is a compact, long-blooming yarrow cultivar bearing flat-topped clusters of small, cherry-pink to cerise flowers with paler pink centers above finely dissected, aromatic, fern-like gray-green foliage, blooming from early summer well into fall if deadheaded. Like the wild species, it thrives on neglect, tolerating poor soil, heat, humidity, and drought once established, and its nectar-rich flower clusters draw a steady stream of butterflies and other pollinators while resisting deer and rabbits. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall to keep the planting vigorous and to control its naturally spreading habit.

common_name: Encore Autumn Moonlight Azalea (Reblooming White Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4-6 hours of direct sun; like other Encore varieties, Autumn Moonlight needs more direct light than traditional spring-only azaleas to rebloom dependably in summer and fall.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with several hours of direct sun for the strongest rebloom; Encore Autumn Moonlight bears large, single, pure white flowers with a soft chartreuse-yellow blotch in the throat, opening in a heavy spring flush and then again in lighter bursts through summer and into fall. Its bright white bloom reads especially well in shaded or evening gardens, where it lights up the understory against darker-leaved companions. As with other Encore azaleas, avoid deep, all-day shade, since inadequate light reduces the summer and fall rebloom cycles that distinguish this series from traditional once-blooming azaleas. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and moist, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer after the spring flush to support later reblooming.

common_name: Osaka Red Ornamental Kale (Rose-Purple Flowering Cabbage)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in mid-to-late summer for fall and winter color and transplant out as temperatures cool; the deep rose-purple center intensifies with each hard frost rather than being damaged by it.

directions: Start seed indoors in mid-to-late summer and transplant into full sun with steady moisture, since ornamental kale needs a long cool season to size up before its color peaks. Osaka Red forms a broad, smooth-edged rosette of blue-green outer leaves surrounding a large, richly colored rose-to-purple-red center that deepens further with each cold snap, giving fall and winter beds and containers a bold splash of color when most other bedding plants have finished. Its round, cabbage-like form and relatively large size make it a strong focal point in mixed fall containers or mass plantings, distinct from the more deeply fringed, feathery kale types. The leaves are technically edible but are grown almost entirely for ornamental display rather than the table; plants hold their color and form through hard freezes and typically decline only when sustained heat returns in late spring.
sources: Takii Seed — Ornamental Kale Variety Notes

common_name: Nagoya White Ornamental Kale (Fringed-Leaf Flowering Kale)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in mid-to-late summer for fall and winter color and transplant out as temperatures cool; the Nagoya series is bred for a finely fringed, ruffled leaf edge that sets it apart from smooth-leaved flowering cabbage types.

directions: Start seed indoors in mid-to-late summer and transplant into full sun with steady, even moisture, since a long stretch of cool weather is what brings out the finest color and form in ornamental kale. Nagoya White forms a dense, finely fringed, ruffled rosette of blue-green outer leaves surrounding a creamy white to ivory center, the deeply serrated leaf margins giving it a lacier, more feathery texture than smooth-leaved flowering cabbage types like Osaka. The pale center brightens as nights turn cold, making it a favorite for combining with darker-leaved companions in fall containers, window boxes, and mass plantings. Leaves are edible but this series is grown for ornamental display; plants hold their form and color through hard freezes and typically decline only when sustained warm weather returns in late spring.
sources: Takii Seed — Ornamental Kale Variety Notes

common_name: Majestic Giant Pansy (Classic Large-Flowered Pansy Series)

planting.note: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, covering lightly and keeping the seed tray cool and dark for germination, then transplant out as soon as the soil can be worked; Majestic Giant also performs well as a fall-planted pansy in mild-winter zones.

directions: Transplant into full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil, and deadhead regularly to keep the long bloom season going strong. Majestic Giant is a long-standing standard pansy series bred for exceptionally large, 3-4 inch blooms in a wide range of colors and bold blotched patterns, on compact, well-branched plants that hold up well in cool weather and light frost. It performs as a cool-season annual, flowering heavily in spring and again in fall in most climates, and in the Gulf South it is commonly planted in fall for color that carries through a mild winter into early spring. Water at the base rather than overhead to reduce leaf spotting, and shear back lightly if plants stretch or thin out during a warm spell to encourage fresh, compact regrowth.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

common_name: ProCut Red Sunflower (Single-Stem Deep Red Cut Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is above 60°F; for a continuous cut-flower harvest, sow a new short row every 1-2 weeks through midsummer, since ProCut Red flowers all at once rather than over an extended period.

directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in full sun and space plants closely, 6-9 inches apart, since ProCut Red is bred as a true single-stem variety that puts all its energy into one flower on one straight, unbranched stem rather than producing side shoots. Part of the industry-standard ProCut cut-flower series, ProCut Red bears deep mahogany-red petals around a dark center on strong, uniform stems, and its pollen-free flowers won't drop pollen and stain fabric or tablecloths, a key trait for cut-flower use. Because plants bloom together rather than over a stretched-out season, succession sowing every one to two weeks through midsummer is the way to keep a steady supply of stems coming for arrangements. Harvest when petals have just begun to unfurl but the central disk is still tight for the longest vase life, and provide support or a single stake in windy sites to keep the tall, top-heavy stems from bending.
sources: Sakata Seed — ProCut Sunflower Series variety notes
